name: Gareth Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on an orthopaedic surgical ward at a big teaching hospital, so it's hips, knees and broken ankles from people who slipped on ice. A day is pain scores, getting people up on a frame the day after surgery, checking wounds and drains, and chasing the physios. I'm on twelve-hour days, three or four a week. It's physical, and my back already tells me about it on the bus home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment someone who came in on a trolley walks to the toilet on their own. What wears me out is the phone, honestly: families ringing, theatre ringing, pharmacy ringing. I share a flat with my partner Owen, who teaches history at a secondary school, so we both come home and complain about paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a better search engine and a typing assistant, and that's fine. I use one now and then to check a drug interaction before I ring pharmacy. I'd tell my mates on the ward it's not coming for anybody's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same, which isn't bad. Ortho is busy all year and they're always hiring. Owen and I have about four months of rent saved, so we're not rich but we're not scared either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and maybe go for my band promotion next year, the senior staff nurse role. I'd keep using the AI tool for quick lookups, the way I do now. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. My worries are my back and the rota, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your back. How long do you see yourself doing this work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another ten years on the ward, maybe, then something with less lifting, like pre-op assessment clinic. Hoists help, but you still end up taking weight at odd angles. Mohammed (the ward manager) did twenty years on the floor and he walks like an old man at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about money worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We split rent and bills down the middle, and we're both on public sector pay scales. The worry would be if one of us got sick, but four months covers a lot.

say: AI is just a **better search engine** and a typing assistant.
It's **not coming** for anybody's job on the ward.
think: Ortho is **always hiring**, so more of the same isn't bad.
He and Owen have **four months of rent** saved between them.
do: Applies for the **senior staff nurse** promotion next year.
Keeps using the AI tool for **drug lookups** before ringing pharmacy.
feel: **Calm**, with his back and the rota as the real worries.
S0.quote: My worries are my back and the rota, not robots.
fieldNote: Two **public sector salaries** and four months saved make him feel secure.
Already uses AI **now and then** for practical lookups.
Long-term concern is **physical wear**, not technology.
Plans a later move to **pre-op clinic** to spare his back.

steps.text: Apply for the senior staff nurse post on the ortho ward
Keep using the AI tool to check drug interactions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it takes the phone calls and the discharge paperwork off nurses. On the union page I'd say the time saved has to go back into patient care, not into cutting posts. That's my line, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm less worried about me than about Owen. Marking, lesson plans, reports, that's exactly the thinking work on your card. My ward still needs someone to get Mr Patel (a hip patient) out of bed, but Owen (my partner) teaches, and his school might decide it needs fewer teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the senior staff nurse course and take on the ward's digital champion role, since I'm already halfway comfortable with the tools. I'd sit down with Owen and work out a budget where my pay covers the rent alone, just in case. And I'd go to the union branch meetings about AI on the wards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. My own job's fine, but the ground's moving under the house, if you like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a budget where your pay covers the rent mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no more takeaways on Fridays and putting the holiday money into savings for a year. Rent's eleven hundred, and I bring home about two thousand. It's doable, just boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Owen say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen says the kids still need someone to stop them throwing chairs, which is true. But Owen's also the one who spends Sunday nights marking, and that's the bit software would eat first. We joke about it, but the jokes are getting shorter.

fieldNote: His worry **shifts to his partner**, a teacher with high thinking-AI exposure.

steps.text: Volunteer as the ortho ward's digital champion for new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now: protect patient-facing jobs and support the people whose desk jobs go. I'd post about a universal basic income, which is a regular payment from the state to everyone, because I think it'd be needed. At work I'd tell people to stay calm, we're still needed for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one that scares me. By 2028 Owen's (my partner's) teaching job is probably gone or cut to part-time, and that's half our money. Then around 2031 the robots arrive, and a lot of ortho is lifting, turning and walking people, which robots are built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Owen in the first month and plan for one income, starting with cutting the car and moving to a cheaper flat when the lease ends. I'd do the pre-op assessment training early, because it's more conversation and judgement. And I'd join every campaign the union runs for safe staffing law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly at night. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes about three years before the robots here. What does that order mean for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the charting and the care plans go first, which is maybe a quarter of my day, and I'd honestly be glad. But it also means I've got about three years before the lifting and mobilising goes too. Three years is short when you're also carrying a partner who's out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what's the first thing you'd give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, straight away, it's three hundred a month with insurance. Then the plan to buy a flat next year, which Owen and I have been talking about for ages. That one would really hurt.

say: Governments must **protect patient-facing jobs** and support people losing desk work.
He'd post in favour of a **universal basic income**.
think: By 2028 Owen's job is likely **gone or part-time**, halving household income.
Around **2031** robots arrive for the lifting and walking ortho needs.
do: Plans for **one income** with Owen in the first month.
Sells the car and moves to a **cheaper flat** at lease end.
Trains early for **pre-op assessment**, which relies on conversation.
feel: **Scared**, especially lying awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: By 2028 Owen's (my partner's) teaching job is probably gone or cut to part-time, and that's half our money.
fieldNote: His alarm comes from **household income**, not his own post.

Gives up the **flat purchase plan**, the most painful cut.

steps.text: Sell the car to save three hundred a month

Start pre-op assessment training within the first year
Join the union campaign for a safe staffing law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan for the people whose jobs change, and let's make sure care stays human where it matters. I'd say it at work, and I'd probably write to my MP. It's a fair warning, so there's no excuse for being unprepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes it manageable for us. Owen could retrain as a special needs teacher or a school counsellor, which is more hands-on. And I'd be well into pre-op or theatre recovery by 2034, when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pre-op assessment training in year two, once the senior post is sorted. Owen and I would agree to save five hundred a month together for three years. And I'd try the hospital's AI documentation tools as soon as they're piloted, so I'm not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a planning way. There's a list on the fridge in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you try the tools early, given you said you usually wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I usually wait until someone else has used a thing for a few months. With five years I'd still wait a bit, but I'd want to be in the second group, not the last. Being last is how you end up out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Owen put off in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying a flat, probably by two years. We'd rather have the savings than a mortgage when nobody knows which jobs survive. Owen's mum would say we're being silly, but she's retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, and governments have no excuse. Fund retraining, keep nurses in charge of care, and look after teachers. I'd say that on the union page and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine for us. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and probably a charge nurse or in pre-op, and Owen would have had time to move into something more human in schools. The only thing that bugs me is not knowing what nursing looks like at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my plan: promotion, then pre-op training in a few years. I'd still try the tools when they arrive. And we'd buy the flat on schedule, because ten years of renting while we wait would be daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly fine. It's like knowing you'll need a new boiler someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that calm plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots doing mobilisation trials on our ward before 2035, I'd speed up. Or if Owen's school froze hiring. Those are my two alarm bells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self starting nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger self to pick a part of nursing that's mostly talking and judging, not lifting. And to save from the first payslip, not the third year. I wasted two years of savings on a car I didn't need.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Owen's job and the lifting part of mine both go inside five years. What would help is real retraining money for teachers and a basic income that kicks in fast, so one nurse's pay isn't holding up a whole flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me would still want to be nurses. I would, I think. A machine helping someone walk again isn't the same as me cheering when they do it.

headlineQuote: A machine helping someone walk again isn't the same as me cheering when they do it.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old orthopaedic nurse** who lives with Owen, a secondary school history teacher.
He uses AI **now and then** and would volunteer as digital champion once tools are proven.
His real fear is **Owen's job**, since teaching has much more thinking work than ward nursing.
He moves from **calm** in the plateau to **alarmed** with two years' warning, then plans steadily with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Owen's income and the lifting in his own job go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** for teachers and a fast **basic income** to support one-nurse households.
